Meriwether Lewis was a nineteenth-century American explorer who co-led the Lewis and Clark Expedition, a landmark American journey of exploration commissioned by President Thomas Jefferson. The expedition traversed the newly-acquired Louisiana Territory, descended the Columbia River to the Pacific Ocean, and mapped the northwestern United States while documenting indigenous peoples, flora, and fauna. Yet his legacy was shadowed by depression, financial troubles, and an early death under mysterious circumstances.

President Jefferson selected Lewis to lead an expedition exploring the Louisiana Purchase after the 1803 acquisition from France. He co-commanded the Corps of Discovery with William Clark, departing from St. Louis in 1804 and reaching the Pacific Ocean in 1805—a journey of over eight thousand miles. They spent winters with the Mandan Indians of the Upper Missouri River and employed Sacagawea, a Shoshone woman, as translator and guide. Her relationships with local tribes facilitated peaceful contact with western peoples and proved vital to the expedition's success.

Lewis documented comprehensive natural history observations, including specimens and descriptions of previously-unknown plant and animal species of the American West. The expedition established American claims to the Oregon Territory and paved the way for westward expansion. The detailed maps and journals proved invaluable for future settlers. After returning in 1806, Lewis was appointed Governor of the Louisiana Territory but struggled with depression and mounting financial responsibility. The government was slow to reimburse expedition expenses, adding to his burdens. He died under mysterious circumstances in 1809 at Grinder's Stand in Tennessee. The official record lists it as suicide, though some historians question the actual circumstances.
